historical_timeline.summary: Fever and chills, possibly malaria or typhoid.
Throat pain and painful swallowing began at Long Branch, New Jersey.
Referred to the throat specialist Dr. John H. Douglas, who called the disease serious and epithelial in character.
Biopsy confirmed cancer of the right tonsillar pillar; judged beyond surgery.
Dictating his memoirs, written to offset the loss of his fortune to a Wall Street swindle, as speaking became painful.
Moved to a cottage on Mount McGregor, New York.
Died of throat cancer at Mount McGregor, days after finishing his memoirs.

claims.statement: Hiram Ulysses Grant was born on April 27, 1822, in Point Pleasant, Ohio, the first child of Jesse and Hannah Grant.
Grant died of throat cancer on July 23, 1885, at Mount McGregor, New York, days after completing his memoirs.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: Grant was a heavy cigar smoker: his tobacco use rose during the Civil War to about eighteen to twenty cigars a day, and he reported smoking nine or ten a day in peacetime.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents heavy cigar use; reported in a secondary medical-history essay.

claims.statement: In June 1884, at his summer home in Long Branch, New Jersey, Grant began to have stinging throat pain and pain on swallowing.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented onset that anchors the synthetic presentation.

claims.statement: On October 22, 1884, his physician Dr. Fordyce Barker referred Grant to the throat specialist Dr. John H. Douglas, who told him the disease was serious and epithelial in character.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Several months passed between the first symptoms and specialist evaluation.

source_links.locator: Biographical note: the fatal illness first manifested itself in the fall of 1884

claims.statement: Grant's physicians recorded a carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar; a biopsy examined by Dr. George B. Elliot confirmed cancer at a consultation on February 19, 1885, and the doctors judged it beyond surgery.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diagnosis that the synthetic modern diagnosis is linked to.

source_links.locator: Abstract: carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar

claims.statement: Swallowing became so painful that Grant often went without food and water; his care was aimed at comfort, with cocaine applied to numb his throat and opiates taken reluctantly for pain, while he kept writing and, by May 1885, dictating his memoirs.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the symptom burden and the era's palliative options; described without graphic detail.

claims.statement: Grant's cancer has been attributed to his heavy cigar smoking; the specialist he consulted in 1884 suggested a link, and cigar smoking is now known to cause cancers of the mouth and throat.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A plausible causal attribution, not a documented finding; the synthetic tobacco problem is linked to it.

source_links.locator: Cigar smoking causes cancer of the oral cavity, larynx, esophagus, and lung

claims.statement: Grant had recurrent severe, incapacitating headaches, interpreted retrospectively as most likely migraines.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not placed on the active problem list.

claims.statement: In 1858 Grant had fever and chills, possibly from malaria or typhoid, and he had periodic fevers believed to have been malaria.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation of a historical fever; not placed on the active problem list.

claims.statement: Grant's father, Jesse Grant, died in 1873 at age 79; his mother, Hannah Grant, died in 1883.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cited source does not give causes of death.

claims.statement: Late in life Grant lost his personal fortune to a Wall Street swindle and wrote his Civil War memoirs to offset the loss and provide for his wife.
In June 1885 Grant moved with his family to a cottage on Mount McGregor in Wilton, New York, chosen for its cool, dry air, where he died.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Sources differ by a day on the arrival date (June 16 or June 17, 1885).

source_links.locator: Left New York for Mount McGregor on June 17, 1885

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week follow-up on the day of the otolaryngology consultation and biopsy

hpi.narrative: Mr. Grant returns two weeks after his first visit, on the afternoon of his otolaryngology consultation. This morning the otolaryngologist examined him with a flexible laryngoscope, which showed an ulcerated lesion of the right tonsillar pillar with a clear larynx, and took a biopsy. The pathologist's same-day frozen section shows squamous cell carcinoma; p16 staining and the final report will follow within a few days. Last week's contrast CT of the neck showed a right tonsillar mass with one enlarged right level II lymph node. His throat pain is unchanged at 5 of 10. He takes the acetaminophen solution two or three times a day and uses the lidocaine rinse when the pain is worst. He manages soft foods and liquids and has lost 1 kg in two weeks. He smoked his last cigar a week ago, on the quit date set at his first visit, and has not smoked since. Varenicline taken without food made him queasy, so he stayed on 0.5 mg twice daily for an extra week; taken after meals it no longer causes nausea. He has noticed no change in mood, sleep, or dreams. He wants a treatment plan quickly so that he can keep working on his memoir.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Grant returns after staging. The final pathology confirmed p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar, and last week's PET/CT showed no distant spread. The head and neck oncology team has recommended chemoradiation, to start in about ten days. The cold he had last week has cleared, apart from a light cough in the mornings. His throat pain is 4 of 10, down from 6 while he was coughing. He weighs 75.5 kg, 2.5 kg below his weight at intake. He saw the dietitian last week and takes soft, calorie-dense foods with two supplement drinks a day. He has smoked no cigars for three weeks and takes varenicline 1 mg twice daily after meals without nausea or changes in mood or sleep. He worries about money and about finishing his memoir during treatment, but still enjoys his writing and his visitors. He has not yet seen a dentist.

documentation.chief_complaint: Runny nose, cough, and low-grade fever for three days

hpi.narrative: Mr. Grant is a 62-year-old man who asked for a same-day visit. Last week the otolaryngologist biopsied an ulcerated lesion of his right tonsillar pillar, and pathology showed p16-negative squamous cell carcinoma. Staging PET/CT is booked for two days from now. He stopped cigars two weeks ago and takes varenicline 1 mg twice daily. Three days ago he developed a runny nose and sneezing, followed by a dry cough. His highest home temperature was 37.8 °C. Several people at a meeting he attended last week have had colds. Home COVID-19 antigen tests on the first and third days were negative. Coughing fits make his right-sided throat pain worse, now 6 of 10, up from 5 last week. He uses the lidocaine rinse before meals and the acetaminophen solution 20 mL up to four times a day. He has taken no other medicines, because he was unsure what was safe. He is still managing soft foods and two supplement drinks a day, and he has not choked or coughed while eating or drinking. His saliva was streaked with blood the day after the biopsy and has been clear since. The urge for a cigar is stronger when he coughs, but he has not smoked. He worries that the cough means the cancer has spread to his lungs.

referral.question: Four weeks of right-sided throat pain and painful swallowing with a persistent lesion of the right tonsillar pillar in a 62-year-old heavy cigar smoker, suspicious for oropharyngeal cancer. Please examine with laryngoscopy, obtain a biopsy with p16 testing, and advise on staging and next steps
referral.urgency: Urgent, within two weeks of presentation; a contrast CT of the neck is booked for next week so the images are ready for your visit
referral.pertinent_history: Right-sided throat pain for four weeks, worse with swallowing and not improving, now 5 of 10. He eats only soft foods and liquids and has lost about 2 kg. A lesion of the right tonsillar pillar is visible on examination. Cigars, about ten a day for more than forty years, inhaling some of the smoke; alcohol one or two drinks a week. He has set a quit date one week from today and started varenicline. Liquid acetaminophen and viscous lidocaine started today for the pain. Blood count, metabolic panel, albumin, and TSH are normal; PHQ-2 1. He wants a clear answer quickly so that he can plan for his family and finish his memoir
questions: Is the right tonsillar lesion a cancer? Please obtain tissue, with p16 testing
Does laryngoscopy show any other lesion of the larynx or pharynx?
What staging is needed beyond the neck CT? I plan a PET/CT once carcinoma is confirmed
Who should plan treatment, and what should primary care arrange before it begins: dental care, nutrition, swallowing assessment, and tobacco cessation?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Grant is seen urgently at the request of Dr. Batiste for five weeks of right-sided throat pain and painful swallowing. The pain is 5 of 10 on liquid acetaminophen and the lidocaine rinse. He manages soft foods and liquids without coughing or choking and has lost about 3 kg in all. He has no voice change, ear pain, breathlessness, or blood in his saliva. He smoked about ten cigars a day for more than forty years, inhaling some of the smoke, and stopped a week ago with varenicline; he drinks one or two drinks a week. He wants a diagnosis and a plan quickly so that he can keep working on his memoir
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Last week's contrast CT of the neck, showing a right tonsillar mass with one enlarged right level II lymph node; the intake blood count, metabolic panel, albumin, and TSH, all normal; and today's frozen section, which shows squamous cell carcinoma, with p16 staining and the final report to follow within a few days

assessment.display: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsillar pillar
assessment.assessment: The frozen section confirms squamous cell carcinoma, and with one enlarged right level II node on CT the disease is at least regional. No second lesion is seen in the larynx or pharynx. The stage cannot be assigned until the p16 status is known, because p16-positive and p16-negative oropharyngeal cancers are staged differently, and until PET/CT has looked for distant spread. His long, heavy tobacco use makes p16-negative disease more likely
Limited by pain rather than by aspiration: he manages soft foods and liquids without coughing. A swallowing baseline is needed before treatment, which will make swallowing harder for a time
About 3 kg so far. Nutrition support should start now, before treatment adds to the loss
One week abstinent. Staying off tobacco improves the results of treatment and healing and lowers the risk of a second cancer
